articles.title: De olho em mercado de R$ 2 bilhões, Swift estreia na culinária japonesa
articles.titleKo: De olho em mercado de R$ 2 bilhões, Swift estreia na culinária japonesa
articles.originalSummary: A Swift, marca da JBS, está entrando no segmento de culinária japonesa com uma linha de produtos voltada ao consumo doméstico. O movimento busca ampliar a presença da empresa em um mercado que movimentou mais de R$ 2 bilhões no food service brasileiro nos 12 meses encerrados em junho de 2025, crescimento de 9% na comparação anual, segundo dados do CREST/Instituto Foodservice Brasil (IFB). A estratégia é aproveitar a demanda por gastronomia asiática e oferecer alternativas ao consumo em restaurantes e ao delivery. O portfólio reúne produtos congelados e semiprontos que permitem preparar refeições japonesas em casa, com opções para consumo individual ou em grupo. Entre os lançamentos estão sashimis de salmão, atum e peixe-prego defumado, já fatiados e congelados, além de tartar de salmão, shimeji, edamame, guiozas de carne suína e vegetais e harumakis de queijo e vegetais. Alguns produtos podem ser preparados em aproximadamente dez minutos na air fryer. “Queremos que preparar uma refeição japonesa em casa seja uma escolha tão prática quanto pedir de um restaurante. Para isso, simplificamos etapas que exigem mais técnica, como o corte dos peixes”, afirma Aécio Patuzzi, diretor comercial da Swift. A entrada na categoria faz parte da estratégia da companhia de ampliar as ocasiões de consumo e fortalecer seu portfólio de marca própria. Atualmente, a Swift mantém mais de 480 lojas físicas e pontos de venda no varejo paulista, além de operar por canais digitais. Os produtos da nova linha custam entre R$ 15,90 e R$ 30,90 e chegam de forma escalonada às lojas, ao e-commerce e ao aplicativo da marca. Para 2027, a empresa prevê ampliar o portfólio com hot roll de salmão, ceviche de tilápia, salmão para poke, tempurá de camarão e mix para yakisoba. articles.title: Bershka inaugura loja de 555 m² no ParkShopping, em Brasília
articles.titleKo: Bershka inaugura loja de 555 m² no ParkShopping, em Brasília
articles.originalSummary: A Bershka inaugurou uma nova loja no ParkShopping, em Brasília. Com 555 m² de área de vendas, a unidade possui quatro salões comerciais e dois acessos, em um projeto que privilegia a integração dos ambientes e a experiência de compra. O espaço reúne as linhas Bershka, BSK e MAN, cada uma com identidade visual própria. A área Bershka combina revestimentos minerais brancos e superfícies de melamina, enquanto a BSK se destaca pelos azulejos rosa. Já a seção masculina mantém uma paleta neutra, com revestimentos cerâmicos em tons claros. A arquitetura aposta em materiais naturais e elementos contemporâneos. O teto, composto por módulos de madeira de bordo e luminárias suspensas, é um dos destaques do projeto. Nos provadores, o mesmo material reveste paredes e cabines, criando um ambiente mais acolhedor. A música também integra o conceito da unidade. Caixas de som revestidas em madeira foram incorporadas aos pilares centrais, transformando elementos estruturais em pontos de destaque. A loja conta ainda com módulos de atendimento assistido nos caixas. A proposta é combinar moda, design e experiência em um ambiente que valoriza a circulação dos clientes e a identidade das diferentes linhas da marca. Em setembro, a marca também inaugurou unidade no Rio de Janeiro . Em março, a primeira loja chegou ao Brasil, no Morumbi Shopping. Lançou, na mesma fase, sua plataforma online, marcando o início da presença no País. Pela plataforma digital da Bershka, os clientes podem verificar a disponibilidade de produtos e localizar peças dentro da loja. Também é possível fazer pedidos online e retirar na loja em cerca de duas horas. O espaço ainda conta com caixas dedicados para devoluções, um ponto de retirada de pedidos online e uma área de self checkout. articles.title: Taco John’s Brings Back Holiday Favorites Nachos Navidad and Apple Grande
articles.titleKo: Taco John’s Brings Back Holiday Favorites Nachos Navidad and Apple Grande
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . For those craving a winter treat, Taco John’s welcomes back one of its most requested seasonal menu items, the Apple Grande. From the comeback of its classic beef chili to the return of Nachos Navidad and fan-favorite Apple Grande, Taco John’s is giving fans plenty of reasons to celebrate the season, and the bold flavors of West-Mex. “The holidays are all about traditions, and at Taco John’s, that includes bringing back the seasonal flavors our guests know and love,” said Kevin Flaherty, Chief Marketing Officer at Taco John’s. “From favorite menu items to opportunities to give back in our communities, we’re serving up the food, value and holiday spirit that make this time of year so special.” For those craving a winter treat, Taco John’s welcomes back one of its most requested seasonal menu items, the Apple Grande. This sweet-and-savory treat features a crispy cinnamon-sugar tostada topped with warm apple pie filling, Cheddar cheese, and cinnamon candy flavored seasoning. Taco John’s is bringing back its Nachos Navidad, a festive, colorful classic featuring crispy red, green and white corn chips fried in-house daily and sprinkled with sea salt then layered with warm nacho cheese, seasoned 100% North American Beef, refried beans, four-cheese blend, diced tomatoes, sour cream, and guacamole. For nearly three decades, participating Taco John’s franchisees have donated a portion of Nachos Navidad proceeds to worthy causes within their local communities, raising millions of dollars to support hundreds of organizations in Taco John’s markets. The beloved holiday tradition brings together great food and the spirit of giving, making every order meaningful. Beyond menu highlights, Taco John’s is spreading even more holiday cheer with special offers* through the in-app TJ Rewards program throughout the season: November 30-December 6 – Cozy Week of Deals: Taco John’s is warming up the season with a week of special offers, giving guests even more ways to enjoy their favorites while celebrating the holidays. December 17-19 – Feed Your Fiesta Rewards Exclusive: Feed your crew for less with deals on sharable items as families and friends come together to make merry this season! Taco John’s is also helping guests give (and get) a little more this season. Now through December 31, guests who purchase $25 in gift cards will receive a $5 bonus card, redeemable Jan. 1 – Feb. 28, 2027. For more information or to find a location, visit www.TacoJohns.com or download the Taco John’s app, which includes additional access to exclusive savings. *Offers are subject to change; latest offers are available in the app. The post Taco John’s Brings Back Holiday Favorites Nachos Navidad and Apple Grande appeared first on QSR Magazine .

The Southern-born fast-food chain is bringing back Krystalmas: A Season of Merry Moments, delivering an entire month of holiday savings, festive flavors and chances to win. From Dec. 1 through 31, Club Krystal members can enjoy a new deal every day on guest favorites, from breakfast biscuits to the brand’s signature square sliders. Whether fueling up for holiday shopping or bringing home a Sackful to share, members can celebrate the season without breaking the bank. Among the deals guests can look forward to are $4 Merry Mornings, featuring any biscuit, small tots and a small coffee during breakfast hours, and Jingle Bucks Thursdays, when Club Krystal members can score Original Krystals for just $1 each, up to five per member. And that’s just a taste of what’s in store, with additional daily deals and surprises waiting to be unwrapped throughout December. “The holidays are all about finding little moments of joy, and we want Krystal to be part of those moments,” said Kaitlin Kees, Senior Director of Marketing at Krystal. “Whether guests are fueling up while holiday shopping or picking up a Steamer Box on the way to grandmother’s house, Krystalmas gives our loyal fans more ways to enjoy their favorites at a great value all season long.” A Chance to Win a Holiday Getaway The holiday cheer doesn’t stop with daily deals. Krystal is teaming up with Coca-Cola to give Club Krystal members a shot at a theme park getaway, complete with tickets and travel funds. From Dec. 1 through 31, Club Krystal members who purchase a Coca-Cola beverage or a Krystal combo with a Coca-Cola beverage through the Krystal app will automatically earn an entry into the Krystalmas Coca-Cola Sweepstakes. Each qualifying order counts as an entry, giving members another chance to win throughout the month. Even More Holiday Savings with the $9.94 Holiday Haul Krystal is extending the holiday savings to all guests with its $9.94 Holiday Haul. With holiday shopping, travel and family gatherings stretching budgets this time of year, Krystal is making it easier to feed a hungry crew without breaking the bank. Available Saturdays and Sundays from Nov. 21 through Jan. 3, the offer includes 10 Original Krystals for just $9.94, a nod to the brand’s 94th year. Unlike the daily Krystalmas deals, the Holiday Haul is available to all guests ordering in-store and online, with no Club Krystal membership required. Guests can join Club Krystal through the Krystal app or visit Krystal.com/rewards to access the holiday offers. For restaurant locations and additional information, visit Krystal.com. Krystalmas offers are exclusive to Club Krystal members Dec. 1–31 at participating locations. Prices, participation, offer limits and availability may vary. articles.title: Software Companies Guarantee Performance. Why Don’t Advertising Agencies?
articles.titleKo: Software Companies Guarantee Performance. Why Don’t Advertising Agencies?
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . For too many years, agencies have kept themselves out of the line of fire. Over the past 12 months, I’ve talked with restaurant marketers across the food franchise space, and a clear theme came through: a wave of new expectations is being placed on them by their brands. They were all pretty unified that they are under tremendous pressure, and the strongest pressure point is showing unit-level performance within 90 days. Unit-level economics is what keeps franchisees, CEOs, boards, and private equity at ease, and marketers are expected to move that number fast. If they can’t show that number moving in the right direction, they will not be granted time to develop new creative that builds brand momentum, improve their tech stack, or address anything else. These are the items marketers used to tackle first to bring cohesiveness and structure to a brand. Now, time limits in the role have pushed them to the back burner. No room to build, no room to fix, no room for anything but survival. Under this pressure, marketers need a new mode of support from their agency partners. They don’t need another report or another promise. They need a partner willing to share the risk, not just the credit, when the results come in. A 150-Year-Old Model The modern agency relationship traces back to Philadelphia. In the 1870s, N.W. Ayer & Son introduced the “open contract,” which put the agent squarely on the advertiser’s side instead of playing a balancing act between channel rep and brand rep. In the 150 years since, the basic advertising agency model for performance and compensation has stayed the same. The agency buys media, reports on deliverables like impressions and clicks, and gets paid either way. We’ve added influencers, creative development, loyalty, and other services along the way, but the model itself hasn’t changed significantly. The Technology Caught Up Everything around that model has changed. Attribution has made huge strides since the advent of Google, and with online ordering, media optimization has become far more effective, which leads to better revenue performance at the location level. POS systems and loyalty marketing give brands a closer touch with their guests, which leads to better activation. Today we can run media location by location, attribute online revenue to each one, and use restaurant data platforms to read the results while factoring in inclement weather and other variables. Influencer marketing is moving toward full attribution, and other media are moving in the same direction. For instance, we are running a social campaign with lead gen activation that sends guests a $5-off-$25 Toast coupon code by SMS, and we’ve validated a 5x return in-store revenue to media spend for this campaign. Stack enough measurable tactics like that together, and you can predict what a location will do. The technology caught up. The agency model hasn’t. Software Figured This Out Years Ago Software companies have long let the product prove itself before the customer carries the full risk. Pilots, 90-day trials, and service-level commitments with credits when the vendor falls short are standard in SaaS. The vendor stands behind what it sells because it can measure whether it delivered. Advertising has not followed, and there is no longer a technical reason why. With food marketers in such a box, isn’t it time for agencies to shoulder more of the burden? What an Agency Guarantee Could Look Like Borrow straight from the SaaS playbook. A brand selects a test group of its locations. Each one gets a revenue goal, measured against the same period last year and agreed by the brand and the agency before any work begins. That goal should cover every channel the location has: dine-in, takeout, catering, and third-party delivery. articles.title: NRF 2027: O que Walmart, Zara, Levi’s, Etsy e Target vão levar ao palco nesta edição
articles.titleKo: NRF 2027: O que Walmart, Zara, Levi’s, Etsy e Target vão levar ao palco nesta edição
articles.originalSummary: Como transformar Inteligência Artificial em vendas? Esta tem sido a pergunta do milhão no mercado. De que maneira as marcas tradicionais podem continuar relevantes diante das mudanças no comportamento do consumidor? E como recuperar o crescimento sem depender apenas de promoções e descontos? Essas são algumas das questões que estarão no centro das apresentações de Walmart, Zara, Levi’s, Etsy e Target na NRF 2027: Retail’s Big Show, que acontece entre 10 e 12 de janeiro, em Nova York, nos Estados Unidos. As cinco empresas estão confirmadas na programação do evento e levarão aos debates diferentes perspectivas sobre as transformações do varejo. Entre os assuntos anunciados estão o avanço dos agentes de Inteligência Artificial, a personalização da jornada de compra, a evolução das lojas e dos canais digitais e a busca por crescimento sustentável. A programação antecipa discussões que interessam diretamente ao varejo brasileiro, especialmente em um cenário de pressão sobre margens, transformação dos canais de venda e consumidores cada vez mais exigentes. Walmart: quando a IA passa a participar da compra Uma das apresentações será a do Walmart, que reunirá David Guggina, CEO do Walmart nos Estados Unidos, e Chris Nicholas, CEO do Walmart International. Na sessão “One Walmart, Many Markets: Leading the Next Era of Retail”, os executivos discutirão como a companhia está respondendo às mudanças nas expectativas dos consumidores em diferentes mercados, com atenção à Inteligência Artificial e ao chamado comércio agêntico ( agentic commerce ). O tema envolve uma transformação na jornada de compra: ferramentas de IA que deixam de apenas recomendar produtos e passam a participar de etapas como descoberta, comparação e seleção. Para os varejistas, o avanço desse modelo traz questões sobre como os consumidores encontrarão produtos, como as marcas disputarão visibilidade e qual será o papel das plataformas digitais nas decisões de compra. Zara: como continuar relevante sem perder a identidade No varejo de moda, o destaque será Óscar García Maceiras, CEO da Inditex, grupo controlador da Zara e de marcas como Pull&Bear, Bershka, Massimo Dutti e Stradivarius. Na apresentação “The Future of Fashion Retail: Staying True, Moving Forward”, o executivo discutirá a evolução do modelo de negócios da companhia e sua capacidade de responder às mudanças no comportamento do consumidor. O enfoque estará na combinação entre identidade de marca, desenvolvimento de produtos, experiência nas lojas e canais digitais. A Zara construiu parte de sua trajetória sobre a capacidade de interpretar as preferências dos consumidores e adaptar seu modelo comercial. Na NRF, a discussão será como preservar esses princípios em um ambiente de consumo que exige respostas cada vez mais rápidas e experiências integradas. Ruby Tuesday's new menu contains approximately 25 percent fewer items and puts greater focus on the company's signature categories. Ruby Tuesday wants customers to remember why they fell in love with the brand in the first place. The casual-dining chain has been serving guests since 1972, building a reputation around its Garden Bar, burgers, ribs, and familiar American comfort food. But more than five decades of history have also brought challenges, including a crowded menu, inconsistent execution, and a reliance on discounts to attract customers. The concept also notably filed for bankruptcy in 2020 and has shuttered hundreds of restaurants over the past decade. Now, the company, with around 160 U.S. locations, according to its website, is making significant changes to its food, pricing, marketing, and restaurant experience in an effort to reconnect with longtime customers and introduce itself to a new generation. CMO Kevin FitzPatrick says the changes respond to mounting financial pressures on consumers and the company’s need to deliver a more consistent dining experience. The previous menu had grown substantially, partly because of limited-time promotions that introduced numerous dishes. That expansion created operational complexity and made it more difficult for customers to navigate the offerings. Introduced nationwide November 17, the new menu contains approximately 25 percent fewer items and puts greater focus on the company’s signature categories. The decision was informed by sales data, customer reviews, and conversations with restaurant employees. FitzPatrick says the company identified dishes that contributed relatively little to sales and could be eliminated without significantly limiting customers’ choices. Some pasta and chicken selections were removed, allowing employees to concentrate on preparing fewer dishes consistently and improving food quality. “I’ve done a lot of consumer research in my past, but like the biggest source of consumer research is sales data. Customers are voting with their wallets, and we had a lot of items that just didn’t have a lot of a lot of reps,” FitzPatrick says. Ruby Tuesday expanded its burger selection with the Jalapeno Smashed and Garlic Parmesan Smashed burgers and brought back the Colossal Burger, a longtime customer favorite. The Colossal Burger had previously returned as a limited-time offering in May 2022, but customers continued requesting it after the promotion ended. The chain also upgraded its chicken sandwiches and entrées to feature eight-ounce chicken breasts and introduced appetizers such as Pretzel Bites, Loaded Fries and Tots, and a Dip Trio. Other signature dishes, including the Hickory Bourbon Salmon and fall-off-the-bone ribs, received greater prominence. The chain previously relied on rotating daily promotions and coupons, a strategy that appealed to its established customer base but required guests to keep track of which offers were available on particular days. Its new Everyday Fresh Meals platform replaces that complexity with consistent pricing seven days a week. Introduced nationally in November, the program features 13 entrées across four price tiers of $9.99, $11.99, $14.99, and $17.99. Each meal includes an entrée, unlimited trips to the Garden Bar, and a bottomless beverage. Selections range from burgers and chicken sandwiches to Cajun Chicken Pasta and a half rack of ribs. articles.title: Smalls Sliders Makes Room for More Restaurants
articles.titleKo: Smalls Sliders Makes Room for More Restaurants
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . A shipping container helped make Smalls Sliders one of the industry’s most recognizable emerging brands. Now, the company is discovering that its signature building can also stand in the way of expansion. Since opening its first restaurant in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, in 2019, Smalls has built its identity around bright orange shipping-container restaurants known as Cans. The compact buildings, streamlined kitchens, and focused menu of cheeseburger sliders, waffle fries, and milkshakes have provided a foundation for franchise growth. But the format comes with real estate limitations. A standalone Can cannot easily fit into a downtown shopping district, an airport terminal, or a college campus. Some communities also prohibit drive-thrus, eliminating potential development opportunities before franchisees can seriously consider them. Smalls is preparing to address those obstacles with its first inline and endcap restaurant formats, which will allow franchisees to open locations in existing retail spaces, shopping centers, and other commercial properties. A rendering of Smalls Sliders’ endcap design. Chief development officer Ryan Crumley says the expansion is a natural evolution of the business, giving operators more freedom to pursue opportunities that previously fell outside the company’s real estate requirements. The shift could open new markets, reduce certain development expenses, and eventually increase the number of restaurants Smalls can open annually. However, the company is not abandoning the Can that helped establish its identity. The new formats will complement the standalone prototype, which will continue serving as the primary vehicle for introducing customers to Smalls. Meanwhile, the new designs will allow operators to consider dense urban districts with substantial pedestrian traffic, suburban shopping centers, malls, and multi-tenant commercial properties. Existing buildings could also offer financial advantages over developing a standalone restaurant from the ground up. An inline or endcap location would generally eliminate the need to construct an entire building shell, parking lot, and utility infrastructure. Those savings could lower the initial investment required of franchisees, although Smalls has not established specific cost comparisons or profitability projections. Crumley says the company expects to learn more as the first locations begin operating. “At the end of the day, our goal and [the franchisees’] goal is for them to be very profitable, and the more you can make that initial investment economical, the better, the faster they get to that point,” Crumley says. The potential savings are only one consideration. Smalls also wants to ensure that opening restaurants in existing buildings does not sacrifice the operational efficiencies that have helped distinguish its business model. The original Can was developed around the needs of employees working inside the restaurant. Its kitchen layout and processes were established first, with the physical structure built to accommodate them. Smalls is applying that same thinking to the new formats, allowing employees to operate in familiar environments regardless of the building type. That consistency is important as franchisees pursue multiple restaurant formats within their territories. A team member moving from a standalone Can to an endcap location should encounter essentially the same kitchen procedures and workflow. The exterior presents a different challenge. Smalls has invested years in making its signature Smorange color and industrial shipping-container appearance instantly recognizable. Recreating those elements in a traditional retail building requires some creativity, especially when landlords have their own architectural standards. articles.title: Com a IA, o cliente sabe tudo. Por que ainda precisa de você?
articles.titleKo: Com a IA, o cliente sabe tudo. Por que ainda precisa de você?
articles.originalSummary: Durante décadas, a autoridade do vendedor veio de saber o que o cliente não sabia: o preço praticado, a diferença entre versões, a letra miúda do contrato. Essa informação continua valendo. Só ficou fácil de conseguir, e quem vivia dela precisa recalcular o próprio valor. O mercado imobiliário americano mostra até onde isso já foi. Segundo a Zillow (2026) , 45% dos compradores que usaram IA na compra disseram ter deixado a ferramenta negociar em seu nome. Mesmo assim, 85% contrataram um corretor. E só 7% o escolheram pela tecnologia. Quando li o relatório, voltei a uma sala de reunião de poucas semanas antes. Eu tinha mostrado ao time comercial de uma grande siderúrgica como o papel de quem vende mudou com a tecnologia. Primeiro, o vendedor sabia mais, e o cliente dava semanas para uma resposta. Depois, o cliente passou a cotar cinco fornecedores ao mesmo tempo, e o prazo caiu para dias. Hoje, ele chega com a decisão encaminhada por busca , rede e IA, e espera resposta em minutos. Na próxima década, aposto que o agente do cliente vai negociar antes mesmo do pedido. A primeira reação foi de ceticismo. Como aquilo entraria na rotina deles? Até eu mostrar o último estágio, em que o vendedor sobe uma camada e cuida do que a máquina não resolve: relacionamento e decisão. Aí as cabeças começaram a balançar, principalmente quando o assunto era a negociação com outras indústrias. A pesquisa mostra onde esse valor foi parar. Quem escolheu corretor pesou conhecimento local, experiência e confiança. A IA levanta o preço do metro quadrado; o corretor sabe se aquele preço faz sentido para aquela rua. E tem um dado que nenhuma planilha resolve: dois em cada três compradores acharam a compra estressante. Informação o cliente já tem. O que pesa é decidir. Agora coloque esse comprador diante de um vendedor treinado no roteiro de sempre: apresentação, características, alternativas. Tudo correto, e tudo o que ele já sabe. Ele precisava de alguém que questionasse as conclusões dele, apontasse o risco que ficou de fora e, quando preciso, corrigisse a IA sem queimar a relação. Vejo a mesma cena numa concessionária, no banco, na consultoria e na negociação entre indústrias. Preparar o time de vendas para usar IA melhora a produtividade interna. Preparar o time para atender quem já usa IA decide a experiência do cliente na ponta. Quanto mais a IA sobe na pré-venda, mais o vendedor precisa subir uma camada. Esse lugar existe, e a sala da siderúrgica, que começou cética, terminou reconhecendo isso. Mas só ocupa quem chega à conversa com algo que a máquina não entregou. Se o seu cliente chegasse amanhã com a resposta da IA na mão, o que o seu time acrescentaria? E me conta, no seu setor, o que o cliente já chega sabendo que, dois anos atrás, perguntava para o seu time? Alexandre van Beeck é fundador da BCK . *Este texto reproduz a opinião do autor e não reflete necessariamente o posicionamento da Mercado&Consumo. articles.title: The Day You’re Closed is the Easiest Room to Sell
articles.titleKo: The Day You’re Closed is the Easiest Room to Sell
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Not every closed day is worth the same money. Sherri Kimes asked in this column how long a menu price should live. Her examples were the Trader Joe’s banana and the Costco hot dog, prices that have lasted for decades because customers carry them around in their heads. I read her piece from the other side of the counter, and the price I kept thinking about is one almost nobody sets at all: what you charge for your restaurant on the day it is closed. Chick-fil-A is dark every Sunday. Most independents take a Monday. A lot of fast-casual dining rooms are empty by eight on a weeknight. Any of those rooms can be sold, once, to a company of thirty that needs somewhere to meet, provided somebody answers the same hour. I run eight event venues in Paris, mostly for companies. The figures below come from 4,048 dated requests that venues using my software have received since March, most of them in Paris. I doubt the behavior changes much between Paris and Columbus. What a Company Actually Buys When a company rents a closed restaurant, it is rarely buying the menu. It wants the whole place, a firm end time, and a kitchen that is cooking for nobody else that night. Nobody at the next table, and the boss can stand up and give a speech without a manager coming over at ten to ask for quiet. Which is why I would not quote a closed Monday as a table for thirty. Quote the house: one number for the room, the staff and the hours, with food on a second line. There is nothing to compare it against, because no customer has ever seen a price for your restaurant on a Monday. In Kimes’s terms this is the most forgettable price you own, and that is what makes it the easiest one to move. Not every closed day is worth the same money. In our requests, 34 percent ask for a Thursday, 21 percent for a Tuesday, and only 10 percent for a Monday, so a Tuesday is worth about twice a Monday. A Monday is not worthless, though: one Thursday request in six says, unprompted, that the date can move. When your Thursday is already taken, that is the moment to offer the day you are closed. The Reply That Goes Out Within the Hour Only 6 percent of requests mention a budget, so waiting to be asked for a price means waiting for almost everyone. The first reply should carry a price, a decision date, and a reason to visit. The price is the easy part on a closed day. There is no service to protect and no regular to displace. The room is simply free, so the number can be decided once and quoted every time. The date is the one most people forget. Of the requests we lost where a reason was recorded, nearly one in four just went silent, and only 17 percent died on budget. Ask the planner when they decide. Then you know when you may call back, and they know when the room goes back on the market. The reason to visit is whatever you leave out. Somebody has to see the room anyway, so keep the layout and the menu for that. An email that answers every question also removes every reason to drop by, and the groups that never drop by are the ones that go quiet on us. Speed matters more than polish here. Just over a third of the quotes that got signed came back within 24 hours of the request. The off-site sits on somebody’s desk for a day or two, and then it is booked somewhere else. What a Closed Day Does to the Week None of this works until the closed day has a price and a team. The price takes an afternoon. The team is harder, because the day you are closed is also the day your people rest, and if you quietly take it from them you will lose more than one event brings in. So I would not try to sell every Monday. Decide in advance how many events a month the house can carry, who volunteers for them, and which day off they get in exchange, and write that down next to the price. articles.title: Stop Letting That Problem Employee Cost Your Restaurant
articles.titleKo: Stop Letting That Problem Employee Cost Your Restaurant
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . You can't tell managers they own the result and then take away their authority the moment it gets uncomfortable. Every restaurant I’ve ever worked with has a Mike. He’s the employee who has been warned about showing up late. He’s been told to follow the recipe. Mike and his manager have had the same conversation so many times they could both recite it from memory. Yet Mike continues to be on the schedule because the owner can’t figure out who else would work sauté on Friday night. How can you avoid the Mikes? Stop comparing the employee to an empty shift When restaurant owners decide whether to keep a problem employee, they compare that person to having nobody at all. That’s the wrong comparison. The real question is: What is this person costing my entire team? That cost never shows up on your P&L. There’s no line item for your best cook getting fed up or your manager losing credibility because everyone knows Mike gets away with things nobody else does. But those costs are real, and they compound. When one person shows up late with no consequence, everyone else starts wondering why they bother being on time. When one person ignores the recipe, the cook who follows it starts to feel like a sucker. Culture isn’t what you put on the wall. Culture is what you allow. Run every problem through “know, can, choose” In some cases, you don’t have the wrong employees. Instead, you have an employee who doesn’t know what’s expected of them. The best way to determine if an employee is the wrong person, ask three questions. Do they know the standard? If you haven’t made the expectation clear, trained it and shown them what “good” looks like, that’s not an employee failure. It’s a leadership failure. Teach them. Can they meet the standard? Some people know exactly what’s expected but can’t perform at that level yet. That calls for more training, more practice or more time. Sometimes it means a different role. A great server may never be a great manager, and a great line cook may not belong in the sous chef job. Do they choose to meet the standard? If they know the closing checklist, can complete it and decide not to, you don’t have a training problem. You have a choice, and choices require accountability. Know when coaching turns into tolerating I’m not telling you to fire someone for their first mistake. Everyone screws up, and people deserve feedback and coaching. But coaching isn’t having the same conversation 14 times. Every time you repeat it with no change and no consequence, you teach that employee your words don’t mean anything and the only consequence is another conversation. At that point, you’re not coaching. You’re tolerating. Back up your managers If you tell your managers to hold the team accountable and then step in with “We really need them this weekend,” you’ve just taught your managers not to manage. Do that a few times, and six months from now you’ll wonder why nobody on your management team confronts anyone. You can’t tell managers they own the result and then take away their authority the moment it gets uncomfortable. That’s pretend delegation. Accept the short-term pain Being short-staffed is not a strategy, and it’s not fun. You may have to cut hours, close a section or work a shift yourself. But temporary pain is very different from permanent dysfunction. Usually, you’ll find when the wrong person finally goes, the team gets lighter and shifts get calmer. Productivity can actually go up with fewer people, because one toxic or unreliable employee can create more work than they accomplish. Put your Mike through the test You already know who your Mike is. Run that person through “know, can, choose” today. If they don’t know, fix the clarity. If they can’t, decide whether more training or a different role makes sense. If they know, they can and they keep choosing not to, stop pretending you have a traini

articles.title: Breakfast Republic to Open Second Location in Coachella Valley, California
articles.titleKo: Breakfast Republic to Open Second Location in Coachella Valley, California
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . San Diego-based Rise & Shine Hospitality Group will officially open its second Breakfast Republic in Coachella Valley, Calif., on Tuesday, November 24, in downtown Palm Springs, joining the Palm Desert location that opened in 2023. Rise & Shine Founder and CEO Johan Engman made the announcement. The new restaurant at 333 South Palm Canyon Drive takes over the space most recently occupied by Impala Bar & Grill. The 3,500-square-foot Breakfast Republic will have a capacity of about 150, including bar seating and patio dining. A fundraising soft opening will be held on Sunday, November 22, from 9:00 a.m. – 1:30 p.m. that is also open to the public. One hundred percent of sales from the day will benefit The LGBTQ Community Center of The Desert. Spots are limited, and interested guests must email Rocky Martinez at rocky.martinez@riseandshinerg.com to request a time slot. The Breakfast Republic menu features comforting breakfast and brunch favorites, including Chilaquiles, Steak ‘n’ Eggs, Breakfast Jambalaya, Bae Mac (mac ‘n cheese), The Cluck Burger, California Breakfast Burrito, and a variety of omelets, scrambles, and benedicts. All eggs are sourced from Vital Farms, whose hens are pasture-raised with at least 108 square feet of space. The sweet side of the menu offers pancakes with varying flavors like Oreo, churro, cinnamon roll, strawberry cheesecake, and blueberry crumble. French toast options include s’mores, banana split, and strawberry & mascarpone. The Rooster Flight for Two allows guests to choose any combination of three pancake and French toast flavors. Gluten-free pancakes and vegan options – such as the Veggie Frittata, Harvest Omelet, Vegan Breakfast Burrito, and Tres Leches Pancakes– are also available. The drink menu has Bloody Maries, bubbles, and breakfast cocktails, including the Morning Mule, Sparkling Strawberry Screwdriver, and Morning Buzz (a take on the classic martini). “Downtown Palm Springs has always been – and always will be – one of the most vibrant and fun areas in all of Southern California,” Engman said. “It truly is a special place, and we are honored that we can bring our ‘cluckin’ good time’ concept to bring even more fun.” Regular hours of operation for Breakfast Republic Palm Springs are 7:00 a.m. – 3:00 p.m., seven days a week. The restaurant will be open on Thanksgiving Day with normal hours. In addition to street parking, there is a parking lot behind Breakfast Republic, and it can be accessed from the restaurant’s cross street of West Baristo Road. Palm Springs marks Rise & Shine’s 12th Breakfast Republic location overall in Southern California, including five in San Diego, three in Los Angeles, and two in Orange County. Two more Breakfast Republic restaurants will open in Southern California in early 2027 – Highland Park (Los Angeles) and Huntington Beach. Rise & Shine also owns three Breakfast Company restaurants, including two in San Diego (Gaslamp Breakfast Company and Mission Valley Breakfast Company) and one in the Los Angeles area (West Hollywood Breakfast Company). A fourth – Greenville Breakfast Company – will open in Dallas in December, marking the group’s first concept outside of Southern California. articles.title: Introducing the Royal Fish Fillet & Caviar Spaghetti at Caviar House & Prunier London
articles.titleKo: Introducing the Royal Fish Fillet & Caviar Spaghetti at Caviar House & Prunier London
articles.originalSummary: Caviar House & Prunier’s Piccadilly flagship introduces new dishes, whilst keeping the firm favourites that have made the restaurant a destination in its own right. The additions bring fresh personality to the offering, from an elevated take on a British classic to a highly indulgent seafood club sandwich. The New Additions The Royal Fish Fillet (£75) takes the humble fish finger sandwich somewhere unexpected. Battered hake served in a brioche bun with melted American cheese and the chef’s homemade tartar sauce, finished with a generous portion of caviar. It’s elevated comfort without losing what made it comforting in the first place. Caviar Spaghetti (£44) keeps things simple with an exquisite white wine sauce gently folded with fresh Prunier caviar and al dente spaghetti. A staple at Prunier’s original Paris restaurant, this dish is a match made in heaven that will please and delight every palate. Watch the dish being made here instagram.com/p/DXPRxz7MlSu . The Lobster & Caviar Club Sandwich (£45) is the dish everyone covets. Half a lobster, boiled egg, tomato, mixed leaves and Emmental, brought together with the chef’s signature Caviar Marie Rose sauce between thick wholemeal bread, served with fries. A showstopper set to become a firm favourite. King Crab & Caviar (£115) rounds out the new arrivals with restraint. Succulent King Crab paired with 10g of Prunier caviar and a green leaf salad, letting two exceptional ingredients speak for themselves. The Favourites Staying Put Some dishes have earned their permanent place. The Caviar Baked Potato (£75), for example, with 30g of Prunier caviar atop an indulgently twice-baked potato, remains one of the restaurant’s most requested dishes. It’s a nod to Jackie Kennedy’s own love of caviar and jacket potato, scaled up for extra indulgence. Caviar & Crisps (£50) continues to hold its title as London’s most talked-about bar snack, presented with 30g of Prunier caviar served simply with lightly salted, hand-cooked potato crisps and a side of crème fraîche. Designed to be shared alongside a glass of perfectly chilled fizz. The all-day brunch menu also remains a firm fixture, with eggs served every way alongside smoked salmon and caviar. Scrambled Eggs & Caviar (£18), Eggs Royale (£20), and The Royal Trio (£22), scrambled eggs with both smoked salmon and caviar, all continue to draw regulars back for breakfast, lunch, or anything in between. For something more elaborate, the Tsarina (£44) brings 10g of Prunier caviar and Balik smoked salmon together on a savoury pancake with crème fraîche. Each new dish follows the same principle that runs through the entire menu: exceptional ingredients, given the attention they deserve, without unnecessary complication. The full menu, including all new additions, is available now at Caviar House & Prunier, 161 Piccadilly, London. Reservations recommended. For reservations or further information, please see www.caviarhouse-prunier.co.uk

articles.titleKo: Introducing Pardeh, A Contemporary Persian Restaurant With International Influences, Now Open In East London
articles.originalSummary: Pardeh , a new contemporary Persian restaurant founded by former theatre set designer, Sahar Gilabadi, officially opened on November 18 , in East London’s Bethnal Green. Located within Empress Works on The Oval, the restaurant brings a fresh perspective to Persian dining, combining traditional Iranian recipes and ingredients with international techniques and influences. With a menu designed for sharing, a considered wine programme and distinctive interiors that bring together industrial architecture and traditional Persian antiques, Pardeh offers a contemporary interpretation of the warmth and generosity of Iranian hospitality. Taking its name from the Farsi word for curtain , Pardeh draws inspiration from the traditions of Persian home cooking and the conviviality of gathering around the table. The restaurant’s kitchen, launch menu and wine list were developed in consultation with Iranian-born chef Yma Apa, formerly of The Drunken Butler and Tehran-Berlin, whose experience cooking across Europe has informed a distinctive approach to Persian cuisine. Rooted in traditional flavours and ingredients, the menu incorporates classical French techniques alongside influences from wider Asian cooking, bringing together familiar dishes and more unexpected interpretations. At the heart of Pardeh’s menu is a selection of signature dishes celebrating the rich culinary heritage of Iran through contemporary interpretations. Designed to be enjoyed across the table, the menu balances the comforting familiarity of traditional Persian cooking with a contemporary, international sensibility. Menu highlights include Green Mango Shirazi , a vibrant reinterpretation of the traditional Persian chopped salad; Saffron Chicken , celebrating one of Iran’s most prized ingredients; and Ghorme Sabzi , a green lamb stew with tahdig, bringing together slow-cooked lamb, fragrant herbs and the distinctive crisp golden rice synonymous with Persian cooking. Alongside these signatures, a regularly changing selection of specials will showcase locally sourced meats, fish and seafood, from leading suppliers such as Fin & Flounder, guided by the availability and quality of ingredients. Complementing the food is a carefully curated wine list, bringing together established European producers, emerging winemakers and lesser-known discoveries. Developed with a focus on independent growers and wines of character, the selection spans accessible everyday bottles through to rarer expressions, with rotating additions to reflect the changing menu and seasons. The cocktail programme takes a similarly international approach, combining classic serves with inventive interpretations incorporating Persian ingredients and flavours. The signature cocktails all nod to Persian flavours, including the arak based Tehran 75, alongside a saffron Martini, and tamarind Margherita Conceived as a welcoming neighbourhood destination, Pardeh offers several distinct spaces designed to accommodate different dining occasions. The main restaurant, seating 50, features two central communal tables for up to 14 guests each alongside more intimate tables for two to four. For private gatherings, a curtain-enclosed dining area accommodates up to 12 guests, available for exclusive bookings with a minimum spend of £750, irrespective of party size. At the entrance to the restaurant, Gilas Wine Bar offers a more informal setting for drinks and small plates. Conceived as a lively standing wine and snack bar, Gilas welcomes guests for a spontaneous glass of wine, a selection of seasonal snacks or an aperitif before dinner, creating an accessible neighbourhood destination in its own right. Towards the rear of the restaurant, a dedicated bar and listening space brings another dimension to Pardeh’s atmosphere. articles.title: André Esteves diz em depoimento à PF que ‘Master era banco inexpressivo’
articles.titleKo: André Esteves diz em depoimento à PF que ‘Master era banco inexpressivo’
articles.originalSummary: O chairman e sócio-fundador do BTG Pactual, André Esteves, afirmou ao delegado da Polícia Federal Albert Pavie Ribeiro que o Banco Master “sempre foi visto pelo BTG muito mais como um cliente” do que como um concorrente. “Era um banco muito pequeno, inexpressivo do ponto de vista bancário”, declarou à PF em 21 de outubro na condição de testemunha. Esteves não é investigado na Operação Compliance Zero e prestou depoimento no inquérito que apura suspeitas de cooptação de dois servidores do Banco Central pelo banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro: Paulo Sérgio Neves de Souza, ex-diretor de Fiscalização e ex-chefe-adjunto do Departamento de Supervisão Bancária (Desup), e Belline Santana, ex-chefe de departamento na área de supervisão bancária. Como revelou o Estadão, a PF intimou Esteves a depor após o nome do banqueiro ter sido citado no depoimento do ex-diretor Paulo Sérgio. Em depoimento de 16 minutos, o delegado Albert Pavie Ribeiro questionou Esteves se, em reuniões com Paulo Sérgio e Belline Santana, os ex-servidores do Banco Central haviam demonstrado conhecimento prévio de possíveis irregularidades apontadas pelo BTG Pactual no Master. O delegado mencionou que, segundo o relato de Paulo Sérgio, parte dos achados apresentados pelo banco já era conhecida pela autoridade monetária. Esteves ponderou que as informações levadas ao BC não eram conclusivas. “Os nossos achados, eles na verdade eram menos achados e mais dúvidas. Nós expressamos aquilo que a gente tinha dúvida, que podiam ser indícios de irregularidade”, afirmou. O banqueiro ressaltou que não tinha acesso ao mesmo nível de informações do BC e que o BTG não chegou a realizar uma auditoria aprofundada sobre o Master. “A gente não tinha a precisão de informações que supostamente o regulador tem, ou mesmo se tivesse uma firma de auditoria, coisa do tipo, que não aconteceu”, afirmou. “Como eu disse, nós não fizemos, não chegamos a fazer o due diligence. O due diligence é um processo longo, envolve várias semanas, empresas de auditoria, escritórios de advocacia, não teve nada disso”, acrescentou. Segundo Esteves, as incertezas identificadas pelo BTG inviabilizaram uma eventual aquisição do Master, diante da dificuldade de dimensionar os riscos envolvidos na operação. “O que nós levamos eram apenas as nossas dúvidas e o fato de que, com aquelas dúvidas, era impossível a gente promover uma aquisição, ou seja, uma solução de mercado, porque nós não tínhamos visibilidade de qual era o tamanho do problema, caso tivesse um problema”, afirmou. Esteves explicou que o interesse do BTG em avaliar uma possível aquisição estava relacionado à experiência da instituição na compra de ativos de instituições financeiras em dificuldades. “Nós temos uma história, um modelo de negócio, a gente é o banco aqui no Brasil, ou na América Latina, mais especializado em ativos estressados”, declarou. O banqueiro citou operações anteriores para justificar a atuação do BTG nesse mercado. “Nós compramos os […] do Bamerindus, do Nacional, o Econômico, o Panamericano, foram várias transações desse tipo”, afirmou. “A ideia de eventualmente adquirir um Master em dificuldades se encaixa nessa linha de negócios. Mas, para isso, você precisa ter uma visão mais construtiva, mais objetiva, o que acabou que não se materializou na nossa análise preliminar”, explicou. Questionado pelo delegado da PF sobre eventuais contatos diretos com Paulo Sérgio e Belline Santana, Esteves afirmou não se lembrar de conversas particulares com os dois. “Eu acho que as interações foram nesse tipo de reuniões, vamos dizer, com outras pessoas presentes. O chairman do BTG situou em dezembro de 2024 o momento em que a instituição concluiu que uma possível aquisição do Master seria inviável. Norma’s Cafe, the beloved DFW institution that has been feeding Dallas families since 1956, continues celebrating its 70th year by doing what it does best, bringing people together around the table. This December, Norma’s will open its newest location on Garland Road at White Rock Lake. The opening honors owner Ed Murph, who passed away earlier this year. Ed believed in good food, family and giving back to the community, there is no better way to honor him than by growing what he built through the decades. “Opening a new location in our 70th year is something we know Ed would certainly be proud of,” said Kurt Metzger, Vice President of Operations for Norma’s Cafe. “More than once during this process, we’ve found ourselves saying, ‘Ed would be smiling down.’ He spent decades making Norma’s a place where everyone felt at home. The best way we know to honor him is to keep growing what he built, with the same heart, the same recipes and the same care for the people we serve in the DFW community.” Norma’s is celebrating the White Rock opening with gratitude! The first 100 guests through the doors on opening day will receive one free chicken fried steak dinner a month for a year. Additionally, the White Rock location looks forward to being active in local community events and charitable organizations, similar to the other five locations. Ed made community give back a key part of his business model, and the company’s commitment is to keep that spirit alive in the years to come. For the last two and a half years, Norma’s has operated a virtual to-go kitchen in the Garland White Rock area, and the success of that business made this brick-and-mortar cafe a clear and optimistic direction. Guests can expect the same menu, recipes and service they’ve trusted for 70 years, from big breakfasts to award-winning chicken fried steak and of course those Mile-High Pies. “This new location is a concrete step towards our future, but with humble reflection on our past. It was a career highlight to have worked for such a Dallas restaurant icon as Ed Murph. His legacy is very important to me and it is an honor to carry that legacy forward,” Metzger said. “Part of the Norma’s magic is seeing just how broad our guest base is. Everyone has a chair at Norma’s table, and we wouldn’t have it any other way! We are humbled by the kind outreach from the future guests of the White Rock area. We look forward to serving them like family for many years to come.” The White Rock location, at 9004 Garland Road, Dallas, TX 75218, opens this December. For more information about Norma’s Cafe locations, or its full-service catering operation, please call (972) 820-5871 or visit: www.NormasCafe.com. A beloved Hispanic snack cake is getting a new spin at Del Taco. Beginning November 19, Del Taco, the nation’s second largest Mexican quick service restaurant*, is teaming up with Marinela, the celebrated Hispanic snack brand, to introduce the Marinela Gansito Shake, a hand-blended creation that takes the iconic snack cake straight from the wrapper to the cup. The new indulgence features an entire Marinela Gansito snack cake blended into a creamy vanilla shake, delivering the cake’s signature chocolate coating, strawberry filling and vanilla-flavored cream to every sip. Rather than simply borrowing Gansito’s familiar flavors, Del Taco hand-blends a full Gansito snack cake into every shake, giving fans a new way to enjoy the treat and experience a playful take on a classic. “Collaborations like this allow us to bring recognizable brands and flavors to the Del Taco menu in relevant and unexpected ways,” said Noah Chillingworth, Chief Marketing Officer of Del Taco. “Gansito has a special place in Mexican snack culture, and incorporating a whole cake into our hand-blended shake highlights that familiarity, offers something new for guests to discover and reinforces our commitment to flavors, experiences and innovation.” “Gansito has been part of Marinela’s story for generations,” said Leslie Vesper, senior vice president of marketing at Bimbo Bakeries USA (Bimbo USA). “Partnering with Del Taco lets us share this beloved treat in a whole new way. We hope this holiday mash-up adds a little extra sweetness to the season.” First introduced as part of Marinela’s early efforts to bring individually packaged cakes to consumers, Gansito has a history with the brand dating back to the 1950s. The snack cake became known for its distinctive combination of chocolate coating, strawberry filling and vanilla-flavored cream, a unique flavor profile that has helped it remain a recognizable favorite across generations. Today, the Del Taco collaboration brings the familiar treat to its menu in a new format, celebrating the fun of mixing favorite foods and discovering unexpected combinations. The Marinela Gansito Shake will be available at participating Del Taco restaurants through Dec. 28, while supplies last. articles.title: Corrieri’s Acquired By New Ownership Team
articles.titleKo: Corrieri’s Acquired By New Ownership Team
articles.originalSummary: Corrieri’s, one of Stirling’s most established independent restaurants, has been acquired by business partners Daniel Harrison, Nick Kourie and Emily Luke, who have committed to preserving the heritage, character and identity of the business. A fixture of Stirling’s food and hospitality scene for more than 60 years, Corrieri’s has built a loyal following and a reputation that extends well beyond the city. The restaurant will continue to trade under the Corrieri’s name, with its existing team and current offering remaining in place. The new owners have no plans for immediate changes, with continuity and business as usual the priority as they take over the operation of the restaurant. The acquisition marks the third business venture for Harrison, Kourie and Luke, who already have two businesses together. Their combined experience across the sector will support the continued development of Corrieri’s while maintaining the qualities that have established its reputation. Daniel Harrison said: “Corrieri’s is a true Scottish institution. It has been part of Stirling for more than 60 years and is a business that people genuinely care about. That kind of connection cannot be created overnight, and it is something we have enormous respect for. “When the opportunity arose to acquire Corrieri’s, we saw a business with an exceptional reputation and a strong place within the local community. Our priority is to protect what makes it special while ensuring it has a strong future. “We are not looking to make immediate changes. The Corrieri’s name, the existing team and the current offering will remain in place, and customers can expect the experience they know and love to continue.” The new owners will work closely with the existing team throughout the transition. The Corrieri family, who have owned and operated the business for more than six decades, will also continue to support the transition as Corrieri’s moves into its next chapter. Daniel added: “We have huge respect for what has been built here and for everyone who has played a part in making Corrieri’s what it is today. “Corrieri’s has a unique place in Stirling, and we are very conscious that we are taking on the responsibility of looking after a business that means a great deal to its customers and the wider community. We hope they will continue to support us as we take it forward.”

articles.title: How Accessible is Your Booking Journey to Every Guest?
articles.titleKo: How Accessible is Your Booking Journey to Every Guest?
articles.originalSummary: Hospitality prides itself on welcoming people and providing excellent service once guests have come through the door. But it’s important to remember that the guest experience starts long before a customer reaches the venue. Takepayments UK Dining Trends 2025 Report highlighted that 54% of diners in the UK prefer booking reservations online, while only 11% rarely make a reservation ahead of time. As such, for many guests, the booking process is the first meaningful interaction with the venue. But, now, consider these scenarios. A wheelchair user books in advance via email, adds a note to highlight their needs, but on arrival discovers that the table plan has them seated upstairs. Alternatively, a parent books on the phone, mentions they’ll require a high chair and enough space to position a pram, but this information was never noted down, leading to an awkward situation at the door. Another potential customer, unable to book online, calls, but no one answers. This frustration leads them to pick a new restaurant. Patrick Clover, CEO and Founder of Stampede , argues that hospitality personalisation needs to extend beyond preferences and promotions to understanding the practical requirements that determine whether a guest feels truly welcome at a venue. Uncertainty Begins At The Booking Phase For guests with additional accessibility requirements, uncertainty begins at the booking phase, raising questions such as: “Will the venue be able to cater to my needs?” or “Will this special requirements note reach the right people?” This uncertainty has been reflected in research within the UK’s National Disability Strategy . The 2025 research highlighted that 73% of respondents cited restaurants, cafés and food establishments as the most inaccessible areas of the hospitality sector. Respondents reported, “they experienced barriers and accessibility issues at each stage of the customer journey and overcoming these barriers came at a cost to respondents in terms of money, energy, time and social interaction”. For example, a wheelchair user may need to call, email or input a note when booking with the establishment to confirm that an accessible table is available, rather than simply following the same booking process as everybody else. Although this creates an additional step for both the guest and operator, it doesn’t necessarily provide reassurance that the requirement will be accommodated on arrival. Accessibility Is Also About Choice Consistent levels of service within this context, therefore, cannot start just when someone comes through the door. Guests need to be able to communicate requirements during the booking process and be confident that their needs will be received, stored and factored in. But operators need to consider the channel for this communication to take place, as well as the process to enable this too. After all, for guests with visual impairments, limited dexterity or lower digital confidence, phoning the establishment may be the preferred, or even only, option. Yet catering to this preference has become more difficult as operators face increasingly lean teams. In fact, the April 2026 4.1% rise in the National Living Wage , accompanied by higher employer National Insurance contributions and other employment costs, has led to operators making teams smaller. UKHospitality figures show the sector lost 170,000 jobs in 13 months. As a result, front of house teams are left balancing serving guests, taking orders, preparing drinks and answering incoming calls. Missed calls can mean missed bookings, but answering them pulls them away from guests already in the venue. Therefore, operators need to consider transformation across all of their outdated booking channels. Personalisation Should Reflect Practical Needs Accessibility and inclusivity also sit within a broader question about how effectively hospitality businesses understand the practical requirements of every single guest. articles.title: Gather Your Flock: Butter Bird’s First Christmas Feast Puts Rotisserie Chicken Centre Table
articles.titleKo: Gather Your Flock: Butter Bird’s First Christmas Feast Puts Rotisserie Chicken Centre Table
articles.originalSummary: Champagne and fries had their moment. This Christmas, Butter Bird, the neighbourhood rotisserie on Blossom Street in Ancoats, is making the case for the pairing that comes next: golden, fire-turned rotisserie chicken and a glass of French Crémant. Its first Christmas feasting menu, Gather Your Flock , runs Monday to Saturday from Tuesday 1st to Thursday 24th December at £45 per person for three courses, with every guest welcomed with a glass of Crémant on arrival. Built for sharing and designed for groups, the menu swaps the stiff office-party set menu for platters passed down the table. It opens with chicken fat popcorn and warm sourdough with chicken butter or roast onion and confit garlic butter , before the main event: a half rotisserie chicken per guest, tea-brined in house and slowly turned over open flame in Butter Bird’s Rotisol Millennium rotisserie and butter-basted until the skin is crisp and golden. The feast comes loaded with sides: rotisserie potatoes with chicken salt , chicken fat roast parsnips with honey and thyme , baked butter mash with smoked cheddar and mozzarella , rainbow carrots with dill crème fraîche and hazelnut vinaigrette , roasted sprouts with Parmesan , red cabbage slaw and proper chicken gravy. Vegetarian guests are served spiced roast cauliflower with celeriac purée and roast garlic , and sage and onion stuffing can be added for £8. To finish, there’s blackberry and apple crumble with proper custard , dark chocolate torte with coffee and vanilla cream , Christmas pudding with brandy cream and winter berry compote , or a choice of three scoops of ice cream . “Christmas should feel like a big family dinner, not a set menu you sit through. Everyone round one table, plates going back and forth, glasses topped up. Rotisserie chicken is made for sharing, and there’s nothing like the first pop of Crémant to tell everyone the celebration has started,” says Joe Akka, owner of Butter Bird. Why Crémant? Made in the traditional method across French regions outside Champagne, with a second fermentation in bottle and time on lees, Crémant brings the same fine bubbles, bright acidity and brioche notes as its famous cousin at a far friendlier price. That freshness cuts cleanly through roast chicken, butter and gravy, which is exactly why Butter Bird built a dedicated Crémant bar into the restaurant. Guests can trade up from their welcome glass to bottles from the Loire, Burgundy and Bordeaux, including Langlois Château Crémant de Loire and Burgundy from Jaffelin , or Crémant cocktails such as the Elderflower and Rosemary Spritz , Blood Orange Spritz and Bakewell Spritz . The restaurant’s weekly Club de Crémant night continues throughout the season. The Gather Your Flock menu is available by pre-order only and is designed for tables of six or more. Bookings are open now at butterbird.co.uk/christmas .

Available for $5.75 each, the new hot chocolates offer two ways to enjoy the seasonal favorite. MilkShake Factory, the neighborhood dessert destination known for its handspun milkshakes and small-batch, premium chocolates, is adding something warm to its menu with the launch of Classic Hot Chocolate and Peppermint Hot Chocolate, available now at locations nationwide. Just in time for the holiday season, the new drinks put a MilkShake Factory spin on a familiar favorite, with each cup topped with whipped cream and a piece of the brand’s signature handcrafted chocolate bark. Available for $5.75 each , the new hot chocolates offer two ways to enjoy the seasonal favorite: Classic Hot Chocolate: A comforting winter staple topped with whipped cream and a piece of MilkShake Factory’s fluffy marshmallow chocolate bark. Available through January 4, 2027. The chocolate bark is more than just a topping. Each piece can be enjoyed on its own, dipped into the hot chocolate, stirred in, or left to melt into the warm drink for an extra layer of richness. It’s a playful addition that brings MilkShake Factory’s more than century-long chocolate-making tradition into every cup, while giving guests a chance to enjoy their hot chocolate however they like. The new offerings also celebrate a tradition that began in Pittsburgh in 1914, when the family behind MilkShake Factory first started making chocolate. More than a century later, chocolate remains central to the brand, from its small-batch confections to the signature bark that now tops each cup of hot chocolate. “Chocolate has been part of our family’s story for generations, so we’re excited to bring that tradition to something as familiar and comforting as hot chocolate,” said Dana Edwards Manatos, Founder and CEO of MilkShake Factory. “We especially love the idea of families making it their own, whether that’s dipping the chocolate bark into their drink or stopping in together after a favorite holiday activity. And with MilkShake Factory’s signature handspun milkshakes, sundaes, and handcrafted chocolates still on the menu, there’s plenty to enjoy for those who prefer their desserts cold. (“The ONE Group” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: STKS) today announced the launch of a licensing program for Benihana Express, its premium fast-casual concept that brings the iconic flavors and culinary heritage of Benihana to a convenient, contemporary dining format. Designed for flexibility, operational simplicity and scalability, Benihana Express creates new opportunities for experienced operators and developers to introduce one of America’s most recognizable restaurant brands to traditional and nontraditional dining destinations. “Benihana is one of the most iconic and recognizable restaurant brands in America, and Benihana Express represents an exciting opportunity to bring the flavors our guests love to more people, in more places, more often,” said Emanuel “Manny” Hilario, President and CEO of The ONE Group. “With its flexible footprint, streamlined operating model and broad consumer appeal, we believe Benihana Express has the potential to become a significant growth engine for our Company and a cornerstone of our asset-light expansion strategy.” Built for scalability and operational efficiency, Benihana Express features a streamlined operating model designed for spaces of approximately 800 to 1,000 square feet. Its flexible format is suited for a wide range of traditional and nontraditional locations, including storefronts, airports, sports and entertainment venues, travel hubs and other high-traffic destinations. Licensees benefit from the strength of the Benihana brand, supported by established brand standards, restaurant design guidance, menu development, culinary systems, training, marketing and supply chain resources. Benihana Express brings the bold flavors and signature hibachi favorites of Benihana to a fast, convenient and craveable dining experience. The menu features premium ingredients, including filet mignon and colossal shrimp, alongside made-to-order hibachi rice bowls, hibachi burritos and signature sauces. Guests can also choose from protein-forward meals, low-carb options, cauliflower fried rice, salads and vegetarian selections, along with appetizers and desserts. Designed for today’s lifestyles, Benihana Express offers the flexibility to dine in, take out or enjoy delivery. articles.title: JPMorgan Chase, Visa e Mastercard confirmam vazamento de dados após ataque cibernético
articles.titleKo: JPMorgan Chase, Visa e Mastercard confirmam vazamento de dados após ataque cibernético
articles.originalSummary: Informações pessoais de milhares de clientes do JPMorgan Chase vazaram na internet na quinta-feira, 19, após fornecedores terceirizados do banco serem alvo de um ataque cibernético. O vazamento não tem relação com a interrupção dos serviços bancários registrada no início desta semana, e os dados comprometidos não incluíam informações de cartões de crédito nem informações pessoais particularmente sensíveis, segundo o banco. Os dados vazados parecem consistir principalmente em endereços de e-mail de clientes do Chase e de alguns funcionários do banco, além de números de telefone em determinados casos. “Tomamos conhecimento de que terceiros que prestam serviços à instituição foram alvo de um ataque cibernético”, afirmou Joe Evangelisti, porta-voz do banco. “Com base em nossa investigação até o momento, acreditamos que os invasores acessaram determinados dados de marketing armazenados por esses fornecedores, que podem incluir nomes e endereços de e-mail de alguns clientes.” Visa e Mastercard também confirmaram o vazamento de dados, mas afirmaram que o ataque não afetou suas operações nem as informações de pagamento dos clientes. As contas afetadas, que somam milhares, representam apenas uma pequena parcela da base de clientes do Chase. O banco possui dezenas de milhões de clientes, enquanto Visa e Mastercard atendem bilhões de consumidores. “Neste momento, a exposição dos dados foi contida, e nossas equipes estão trabalhando com o fornecedor para prestar assistência aos titulares de cartões afetados, conforme necessário”, afirmou Seth Eisen, porta-voz da Mastercard. O ataque cibernético não está relacionado ao incidente ocorrido no Chase no início desta semana, quando uma falha de software provocou interrupções em alguns dos serviços bancários da instituição. No entanto, o episódio é o mais recente de uma série de problemas tecnológicos que afetaram diferentes setores da economia global, desde a suspensão de voos até a indisponibilidade de serviços básicos de e-mail e calendário da Microsoft. Conteúdo traduzido com auxílio de Inteligência Artificial, revisado e editado pela Redação do Broadcast, sistema de notícias em tempo real do Grupo Estado. Com Associated Press. articles.title: Anthropic estreia em Wall Street com alta de 17% e se torna 12ª empresa mais valiosa do mundo
articles.titleKo: Anthropic estreia em Wall Street com alta de 17% e se torna 12ª empresa mais valiosa do mundo
articles.originalSummary: A Anthropic encerrou sua estreia em Wall Street nesta quinta-feira como a 12ª empresa mais valiosa do mundo, com capitalização de mercado de US$ 1,271 trilhão, segundo o ranking do CompaniesMarketCap. As ações da companhia de inteligência artificial (IA) saltaram 17,07%, a US$ 97,17, ante o preço de US$ 83 fixado na oferta pública inicial (IPO). Com isso, a Anthropic ultrapassou a Berkshire Hathaway, avaliada em US$ 1,215 trilhão, e ficou logo atrás da Tesla, com valor de mercado de US$ 1,479 trilhão. A empresa vendeu 980 milhões de ações na operação, acima das 825 milhões inicialmente previstas. Considerando a opção de lote adicional, a captação poderá atingir cerca de US$ 94 bilhões, superando os US$ 86 bilhões levantados pela SpaceX em junho. Contrastando com o entusiasmo com a estreia da Anthropic, as ações da SpaceX, de Elon Musk, recuaram 3,53% nesta quinta-feira, a US$ 138,43. Na B3, a estreia dos Brazilian Depositary Receipts (BDRs) da Anthropic superou o volume financeiro da Space X em seu momento de chegada à Bolsa. Estadão Conteúdo com informações da Dow Jones Newswires. articles.originalSummary: 한국식자재유통앤급식협회(회장 양송화, 이하 식자재유통앤급식협회)는 국회 농림축산식품해양수산위원회 소속 더불어민주당 임미애 국회의원실과 공동으로 19일 여의도 국회의원회관 제4간담회의실에서 ‘농업과 식재료유통산업 상생 토론회’를 개최했다.이번 토론회는 농업 생산자와 식재료 유통기업 간의 실질적인 상생 모델을 모색하고 지속가능한 먹거리 유통 생태계 조성을 위한 정책 및 입법 과제를 도출하기 위해 마련됐다.토론회는 양송화 식자재유통앤급식협회 회장의 환영사를 시작으로 임미애(더불어민주당) 의원의 개회사, 김선교·신성범 의원(국민의힘) 축사

articles.title: Menos área para lojas, mais motivos para ir: a estratégia de varejo da Coreia do Sul
articles.titleKo: Menos área para lojas, mais motivos para ir: a estratégia de varejo da Coreia do Sul
articles.originalSummary: Em Yeouido, distrito financeiro de Seul, Coreia do Sul, o The Hyundai Seoul representa uma mudança no modelo tradicional de loja de departamentos. Inaugurado em 2021, o empreendimento combina compras com jardins, exposições, restaurantes e eventos temporários. O shopping também ganhou projeção entre brasileiros por aparecer em Rainha das Lágrimas. Na série, o espaço serve de cenário para a loja de departamentos do grupo Queens. A prefeitura de Seul incluiu o local entre os pontos de filmagem da produção em seu projeto turístico “Soul Spot”. A estratégia parte de uma decisão pouco comum no varejo: reservar menos espaço para lojas convencionais e mais para o público. Dos 89,1 mil metros quadrados de área total, cerca de 51% são destinados a lojas. Os outros 49% abrigam áreas de descanso, paisagismo interno e circulação. Na época da inauguração, a Hyundai informou que a proporção de área comercial era inferior à média de 65% de suas outras lojas de departamento. O projeto também foi concebido para permitir a entrada de luz natural em todos os andares, com grandes aberturas internas, jardins e uma cascata artificial de 12 metros no primeiro piso. A principal área verde é o Sounds Forest, jardim interno no quinto andar, com aproximadamente 3,3 mil metros quadrados. No balanço dos cinco anos do shopping, a Hyundai informou que os visitantes permanecem ali, em média, 37 minutos – cerca de nove vezes mais do que o tempo médio de permanência nas lojas de moda, estimado pela empresa em quatro minutos. O espaço funciona como área de descanso e também como atração: visitantes podem passear pelo jardim, tirar fotos ou simplesmente fazer uma pausa durante a visita. Os números de público dão uma dimensão do alcance da proposta. Nos três primeiros anos, o The Hyundai Seoul recebeu 126 milhões de visitas, de acordo com dados da empresa publicados pelo The Korea Herald. O dado representa visitas acumuladas, e não necessariamente pessoas diferentes. Naquele período, visitantes com menos de 40 anos correspondiam a 58% do público. Em seu balanço de cinco anos, a Hyundai informou que os consumidores de 20 e 30 anos responderam por 58% das vendas em 2025. O impacto também se estendeu aos arredores. Dados da prefeitura de Seul citados pelo The Korea Herald mostram que o fluxo de visitantes em Yeouido nos fins de semana, que em 2020 costumava atingir de 30 mil a 50 mil pessoas, chegou a aproximadamente 120 mil em abril de 2022, depois da abertura do shopping e da retirada das restrições da pandemia. O número se refere à área de Yeouido, não apenas ao The Hyundai Seoul, mas ajuda a ilustrar como uma grande atração comercial pode contribuir para movimentar um distrito de escritórios também nos fins de semana. Pop-ups como motivo para voltar A programação de pop-ups é uma das ferramentas usadas para manter o shopping em evidência. Os eventos podem apresentar marcas de moda, produtos limitados, personagens, artistas e conteúdos de entretenimento por períodos curtos. No balanço de cinco anos, a Hyundai contabilizou cerca de 1.892 pop-ups realizados no The Hyundai Seoul, incluindo mais de 660 em 2025. A empresa apresenta a frequência de eventos como uma forma de acompanhar a velocidade com que mudam as tendências entre os consumidores mais jovens. O resultado aparece tanto no fluxo quanto nas vendas. Segundo dados divulgados pela Hyundai, cerca de 75% dos clientes que compraram em pop-ups eram do grupo chamado MZ – millennials e geração Z. Até o terceiro aniversário do shopping, os eventos atraíam mais de dois milhões de clientes por ano. No mesmo período, a empresa informou que os pop-ups e o aumento de fluxo associado a eles ajudaram o The Hyundai Seoul a ultrapassar 1 trilhão de wons sul-coreanos em vendas em dois anos e nove meses de operação. A programação também é distribuída por áreas específicas, como o Creative Ground, no subsolo 2, voltado a marcas e conteúdos ligados à cultura jovem, e o EPIC SEOUL, espaço de pop-ups e exposições imersivas com re
